Naguib Mahfouz was an Egyptian novelist from Cairo and, in 1988, the first writer in Arabic to win the Nobel Prize in Literature.

He worked most of his life as a civil servant and wrote in the evenings. He brought the realist novel into Arabic and set his stories in the alleys and cafés of old Cairo.

  • The Cairo Trilogy (1956 to 1957) follows one family from the 1919 revolution against British rule to the Second World War.
  • Children of Gebelawi (1959) retells the stories of Adam, Moses, Jesus and Muhammad as an allegory of one Cairo street; it was banned in Egypt for decades.
  • Later novels such as Miramar look at life under Nasser.

He supported peace with Israel after Sadat's treaty, and Islamists called him an apostate. In 1994 a militant stabbed him in the neck outside his home; he survived, but could barely write by hand afterwards. Many of his books became films, some made at Studio Misr.
sum: Naguib Mahfouz was an Egyptian novelist from Cairo and, in 1988, the first writer in Arabic to win the Nobel Prize in Literature.
